title: Lec 01 — Anatomy of the Heart
subtitle: Week 01 · Lec 01 · Anatomy of the Heart | 20 questions

questions.text: A medical student is reviewing thoracic anatomy before a lab practical. The heart, its pericardial sac, the adjacent roots of the great vessels, and the phrenic nerves are all said to reside in which compartment of the mediastinum?
options: Anterior mediastinum
Posterior mediastinum
Middle mediastinum
Superior mediastinum
questions.explanation:
The middle mediastinum (C) is where the heart resides — it is one of three subdivisions of the inferior mediastinum and contains the pericardial sac, heart, roots of the great vessels, and phrenic nerves.

The thoracic mediastinum is first divided by the transverse thoracic plane (passing through the sternal angle anteriorly and the T4–T5 disc posteriorly) into the superior mediastinum above and the inferior mediastinum below. The inferior mediastinum is then subdivided into three regions: the anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and the pericardial sac), the middle mediastinum (the heart itself), and the posterior mediastinum (behind the heart, containing the esophagus, descending aorta, and thoracic duct).

The anterior mediastinum lies in front of the pericardium and contains the thymus and connective tissue — not the heart. The posterior mediastinum sits behind the heart and pericardium — a common site for neurogenic tumors, not cardiac structures. The superior mediastinum is above the transverse thoracic plane and contains the trachea, great vessels, and esophagus as they pass from the neck; the heart does not extend above the sternal angle.

questions.text: During a physical examination tutorial, the instructor asks students to identify a single surface landmark that simultaneously marks the articulation of the second rib anteriorly and corresponds to the T4–T5 intervertebral disc posteriorly. Which landmark satisfies both criteria?
options: Sternal angle (angle of Louis)
Xiphoid process
Suprasternal (jugular) notch
Midsternal line
questions.explanation:
The sternal angle (angle of Louis) (A) is the junction of the manubrium and the sternal body; it articulates with the second rib cartilage and lies in the same transverse plane as the T4–T5 intervertebral disc posteriorly.

The sternal angle is the single most important surface reference point in the anterior thorax. Anteriorly, the 2nd costal cartilage attaches here, making it the starting point for rib counting during physical examination. Posteriorly, this same horizontal plane passes through the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5 — which also marks the aortic arch, the tracheal bifurcation, and the boundary between the superior and inferior mediastina. Knowing this single landmark orientates the entire thoracic cavity.

The xiphoid process is at the inferior end of the sternum, marking roughly the T9–T10 level — far below the 2nd rib. The suprasternal notch is the superior border of the manubrium, corresponding approximately to T2 — above the sternal angle. The midsternal line is a vertical reference line, not a horizontal plane, and cannot mark either the 2nd rib or the T4–T5 disc.

questions.text: A 26-year-old motorcyclist sustains a direct handlebar impact to the anterior chest wall. Which cardiac chamber is most directly at risk of contusion because it forms the majority of the sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart?
options: Left atrium
Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Right atrium
questions.explanation:
The right ventricle (B) forms the majority of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart and lies immediately posterior to the sternum and costal cartilages, making it the chamber most vulnerable to blunt anterior chest trauma.

The anterior surface of the heart faces the sternum and anterior thoracic wall. Because the right ventricle occupies most of this surface, any direct blow to the precordium — from a steering wheel, handlebars, or fist — strikes the right ventricle first. Myocardial contusion from such trauma can cause dysrhythmias and right heart dysfunction.

The left atrium forms the base (posterior surface) of the heart and abuts the esophagus — it is the most posterior chamber and is protected from anterior impacts. The left ventricle forms the left pulmonary and diaphragmatic surfaces, not the anterior surface. The right atrium forms the right pulmonary surface, which faces the right lung, not the anterior chest wall.

Slide 10 · Transcript 05:42

questions.text: A surgeon examining the inferior aspect of the heart during a coronary bypass procedure identifies the surface resting on the diaphragm. Which chamber constitutes the majority of this diaphragmatic surface?
options: Right atrium
Left atrium
Right ventricle
Left ventricle
questions.explanation:
The left ventricle (D) makes up the majority of the diaphragmatic (inferior) surface of the heart, with the right ventricle contributing a smaller portion along its right margin.

The diaphragmatic surface rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm and is also referred to as the inferior surface. It is formed mainly by the left ventricle, with the right ventricle contributing along the right side. This surface is clinically relevant because inferior-wall myocardial infarctions (typically from RCA occlusion) affect the left ventricular territory here, and the middle cardiac vein and posterior descending artery run across it in the posterior interventricular sulcus.

The right atrium forms the right pulmonary surface (facing the right lung), not the diaphragmatic surface. The left atrium forms the posterior surface (base) of the heart, which faces posteriorly toward the esophagus — not downward toward the diaphragm. The right ventricle primarily forms the anterior (sternocostal) surface; it contributes only partially to the diaphragmatic surface.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes a function the pericardium serves in normal cardiac physiology?
options: It generates action potentials that initiate ventricular contraction
It propels oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins into systemic circulation
It lubricates the outer surface of the heart, allowing frictionless movement during each contraction
It regulates the opening and closing of the atrioventricular valves during systole
questions.explanation:
Lubrication (C) is one of the four recognized functions of the pericardium — the serous pericardial layers produce a thin film of fluid that allows the visceral and parietal surfaces to glide smoothly against each other with every heartbeat.

The pericardium performs four main functions: (1) it fixes the heart in place within the mediastinum via fibrous attachments; (2) it prevents overfilling of the heart; (3) it lubricates the outer cardiac surface so contraction and relaxation occur without friction; and (4) it protects the heart from spread of infection from adjacent structures. When the serous surfaces become inflamed (pericarditis), lubrication fails and the roughened surfaces create the audible pericardial friction rub.

Action potential generation is the function of the cardiac conduction system (SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers), not the pericardium. Propelling oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation is the job of the left ventricle. Regulating AV valve opening and closing is accomplished by the papillary muscles and chordae tendineae, not the pericardium.

questions.text: A 35-year-old man arrives in the emergency department after a stab wound to the left chest. Bedside ultrasound shows blood rapidly accumulating inside the pericardial sac. Within minutes his blood pressure drops to 70/40 mm Hg and heart sounds are muffled. Which property of the fibrous pericardium most directly explains why this acute hemorrhage produces life-threatening cardiac compression?
options: It is tough and relatively inelastic, preventing rapid expansion to accommodate the sudden fluid increase
It is innervated by the phrenic nerve, triggering a vasovagal reflex that drops blood pressure
It is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm, physically compressing the ventricles with each breath
It fuses with the visceral serous layer under pressure, obliterating the pericardial cavity
questions.explanation:
The fibrous pericardium's relative inelasticity (A) is the critical property: because it cannot rapidly stretch, any acute fluid accumulation immediately raises intrapericardial pressure and compresses the cardiac chambers, impairing diastolic filling and reducing cardiac output.

The fibrous pericardium is the tough, connective-tissue outer layer of the pericardial sac. It is described as “relatively fixed” — it does not expand easily. In a slowly developing pericardial effusion (chronic), the pericardium has time to gradually stretch and accommodate the fluid volume without critically elevating intrapericardial pressure. In an acute hemorrhage, no such accommodation occurs: pressure rises rapidly, compresses the thin-walled right atrium and ventricle first, prevents diastolic filling, and drops cardiac output — the hallmarks of cardiac tamponade.

Phrenic nerve innervation carries somatic pain from the pericardium to the C3–C5 dermatomes (shoulder, lateral neck) but does not trigger the hemodynamic collapse of tamponade. Diaphragmatic attachments anchor the heart’s position and transmit respiratory pressure changes, but they do not directly compress the ventricles in tamponade. The fibrous pericardium is a single-layered structure; it does not fuse with the serous layers — serous layer apposition is a consequence of effusion, not a cause of tamponade.

Slide 13 · Transcript 08:45

questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with viral pericarditis reports sharp chest pain that radiates to her left shoulder and the lateral aspect of her neck. Which nerve, and at which spinal cord levels, carries the somatic pain afferents from the fibrous and parietal serous pericardium that produce this referral pattern?
options: Vagus nerve (CN X), brainstem to thorax
Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)
Intercostal nerves (T1–T6)
Greater splanchnic nerve (T5–T9)
questions.explanation:
The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) (B) innervates the fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer of the serous pericardium; its afferents refer pain to the C3–C5 dermatomes, which include the supraclavicular region and lateral neck.

The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm and carries its fibers from spinal segments C3, C4, and C5 (“C3, 4, 5, keeps the diaphragm alive”). En route to the diaphragm, it passes through the fibrous pericardium and innervates the pericardial layers. When the pericardium is inflamed, nociceptive signals travel centrally along the phrenic nerve to C3–C5 spinal segments, which also receive cutaneous input from the shoulder and lateral neck — producing the classic referred pain of pericarditis at those locations.

The vagus nerve (CN X) carries visceral afferents for cardiac reflexes (baroreceptor and chemoreceptor signals), not somatic pain from the pericardial layers — vagal pain referral goes to the ear and jaw, not the shoulder. Intercostal nerves innervate the chest wall and parietal pleura; they do not innervate the pericardium. The greater splanchnic nerve is a sympathetic visceral nerve (T5–T9) that carries pain from abdominal organs, not the thoracic pericardium.

questions.text: During a cardiac dissection, a student identifies a groove that encircles the heart between two groups of chambers. The professor explains that this external groove is the surface representation of an internal anatomical boundary. Which internal structure does the coronary sulcus mark on the external surface of the heart?
options: The interventricular septum separating the right and left ventricles
The course of the posterior interventricular artery along the posterior wall
The junction between the pulmonary trunk and the ascending aorta
The atrioventricular septum separating the atria from the ventricles
questions.explanation:
The coronary sulcus (D) is the external surface groove that corresponds to the internal atrioventricular septum — when you see this groove on the outside of the heart, it marks the boundary between the atrial and ventricular chambers within.

The coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus wraps completely around the heart, sitting between the atria superiorly and the ventricles inferiorly. It serves as the external landmark for the internal AV septum. Clinically, the coronary sulcus is important because it houses the major coronary vessels: the right coronary artery travels in it anteriorly and inferiorly, and the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery travels in it posteriorly. Recognizing the sulcus during dissection helps identify these vessels and their position relative to the valve plane.

The interventricular septum, which separates the two ventricles, is marked externally by the anterior and posterior interventricular sulci — distinct grooves that run vertically on the front and back of the heart, not the circumferential coronary sulcus. The posterior interventricular artery runs in the posterior interventricular sulcus, not in the coronary sulcus. The pulmonary trunk and ascending aorta are great vessels that emerge from the heart base; the groove between them is the transverse pericardial sinus, not the coronary sulcus.

questions.text: Examining the interior of the right atrium on a cadaveric specimen, a student finds a smooth, vertical muscular ridge that runs from the opening of the superior vena cava inferiorly to the opening of the inferior vena cava. The pacemaker of the heart is embedded at the superior end of this ridge where the SVC enters the chamber. Which structure is the student examining?
options: Fossa ovalis
Pectinate muscles
Crista terminalis
Moderator band
questions.explanation:
The crista terminalis (C) is the smooth vertical muscular ridge extending from the SVC to IVC inside the right atrium, and the sinoatrial (SA) node — the heart’s primary pacemaker — is located at its superior end where the SVC enters.

The crista terminalis divides the right atrium into two regions: the smooth posterior wall (derived from the sinus venosus) and the rough anterior wall, which bears the parallel muscular ridges called pectinate muscles. The pectinate muscles radiate from the crista terminalis like teeth on a comb. The SA node sits in the superior portion of the crista terminalis, right at the SVC orifice, and is supplied by the SA nodal branch of the right coronary artery. From the SA node, the electrical impulse spreads across the atria, depolarizes the AV node, and continues through the His–Purkinje system to the ventricles.

The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression on the interatrial septum, representing the remnant of the embryonic foramen ovale — it is not a ridge and does not run between the venae cavae. The pectinate muscles are the rough parallel ridges that fan out from the crista terminalis; they are the result of the ridge, not the ridge itself. The moderator band is found in the right ventricle, not the right atrium.

questions.text: During a right ventricle dissection, a demonstrator points to a muscular bundle that spans from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. She notes that this structure contains specialized cardiac conduction tissue that allows rapid signal delivery to the anterior papillary muscle. Which structure is being described?
options: Moderator band
Chordae tendineae
Crista terminalis
Fossa ovalis
questions.explanation:
The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) (A) is the muscular structure unique to the right ventricle that extends from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle and carries right bundle branch fibers across the ventricular cavity.

The moderator band has two functions: anatomically, it bridges the gap between the interventricular septum and the anterior papillary muscle base; conductively, it carries fibers from the right bundle branch, allowing the electrical impulse to reach the anterior papillary muscle rapidly. This ensures the anterior papillary muscle contracts at the onset of systole, tensioning the chordae tendineae before right ventricular pressure rises and preventing tricuspid regurgitation. During dissection, the moderator band is the reliable landmark for identifying which papillary muscle is the anterior one.

Chordae tendineae are fibrous cords connecting the papillary muscle tips to the valve leaflets — they run between the muscle apex and the valve, not from the septum to the papillary muscle base, and carry no conduction tissue. The crista terminalis is a right atrial structure, not a ventricular one. The fossa ovalis is an interatrial septal depression, not found in the right ventricle.

questions.text: A surgeon operating on the right side of the heart needs to inventory the valve leaflets and papillary muscles of the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve before repairing a traumatic rupture. Which of the following correctly describes the anatomy of the tricuspid valve and its associated papillary muscles?
options: Two leaflets (anterior and posterior) supported by two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior)
Three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) supported by three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal)
Three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) supported by two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial)
Two leaflets (anterior and posterior) supported by three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal)
questions.explanation:
The tricuspid valve has three leaflets — anterior, posterior, and septal (B) — and three corresponding papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal) that arise from the right ventricular walls and connect to the leaflets via chordae tendineae.

The name “tricuspid” reflects the three cusps (leaflets). Each leaflet is named by its position: the anterior leaflet faces the sternum, the posterior leaflet faces the diaphragm, and the septal leaflet attaches near the interventricular septum. Three papillary muscles share the same positional names (anterior, posterior, and septal). The anterior papillary muscle is identifiable by its attachment to the moderator band. During systole, all three papillary muscles contract simultaneously, pulling the chordae tendineae taut and preventing the leaflets from prolapsing back into the right atrium.

Two leaflets (anterior and posterior) with two papillary muscles is the anatomy of the left ventricular mitral valve, not the tricuspid. Three leaflets with only two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial) is also the mitral valve pattern: the left ventricle has two large papillary muscles regardless of the three-leaflet tricuspid count. Two leaflets with three papillary muscles describes no cardiac valve in this lecture.

Slide 30 · Transcript 26:28

questions.text: A cardiologist reviewing left ventricular anatomy with students notes that the left atrioventricular valve has fewer leaflets and fewer papillary muscles than its right-sided counterpart. Which of the following correctly describes the mitral valve and its left ventricular papillary muscle anatomy?
options: Three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) and three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal)
Three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) and two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial)
Two leaflets (anterior and posterior) and three papillary muscles
Two leaflets (anterior and posterior) and two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior)
questions.explanation:
The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two leaflets — anterior and posterior (D) — and the left ventricle has two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior, also called anterolateral and posteromedial) that attach to the leaflets via chordae tendineae.

The name “bicuspid” reflects its two cusps; the alternate name “mitral” comes from its resemblance to a bishop’s mitre. The anterior leaflet is the larger of the two and sits adjacent to the aortic valve. The left ventricle contains two large papillary muscles: the anterior (anterolateral) and posterior (posteromedial). Notably, the posteromedial papillary muscle receives its blood supply solely from the posterior descending artery, making it uniquely vulnerable to ischemia in inferior-wall myocardial infarction, which can cause acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture.

Three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) with three papillary muscles describes the right ventricular tricuspid apparatus, not the left side. Three leaflets with two papillary muscles mixes the right-side leaflet count with the left-side muscle count — incorrect for either valve. Two leaflets with three papillary muscles does not describe any cardiac valve anatomy in this lecture.

Slide 36 · Transcript 31:37

questions.text: A physiology instructor explains that the two types of cardiac valves differ fundamentally in how they open and close. One type requires active muscle contraction to remain shut during systole, while the other closes automatically as blood fills its cup-shaped cusps during diastole. Which statement correctly distinguishes the atrioventricular (AV) valves from the semilunar valves?
options: AV valves close during diastole when papillary muscles contract; semilunar valves open during systole by passive filling of their cusps
Both AV and semilunar valves are active: each requires papillary muscle contraction for closure, but semilunar valves also have chordae tendineae
AV valves are active — papillary muscles contract during systole, pulling chordae tendineae to keep leaflets shut; semilunar valves are passive — backflowing blood fills their cusps and closes them
Both AV and semilunar valves are passive: closure depends entirely on the pressure gradient between the chambers without muscle involvement
questions.explanation:
AV valves are active (C) — closure during systole depends on papillary muscle contraction pulling the chordae tendineae to hold leaflets shut and prevent prolapse — while semilunar valves are passive, closing automatically when blood flows back and fills their concave cusps during diastole.

The atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) guard the atrial-ventricular junctions. During systole, as ventricular pressure rises, the papillary muscles contract in tandem with the ventricular myocardium, tensioning the chordae tendineae and preventing the leaflets from being pushed into the atria (prolapse or regurgitation). This is an active, muscle-driven process. The semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) have no chordae tendineae and no papillary muscle connections. They close passively: during diastole, blood attempts to flow back toward the relaxing ventricles, fills the concave cusps, and the weight and pressure of the pooled blood forces the cusps together, sealing the outlet.

The first option reverses the timing: AV valves close during systole (not diastole), and semilunar valves do not close by filling — they close when blood falls back during diastole, not opens. Semilunar valves do not have chordae tendineae in any scenario — the entire point of their passive mechanism is the absence of supporting cords. Both valves being passive is incorrect because AV valve competence genuinely requires active papillary muscle tension.

Slide 32 · Transcript 29:36

questions.text: A cardiology student and her study partner are reviewing the cardiac cycle. Her partner argues there must be a brief moment when all four cardiac valves are simultaneously open to allow continuous blood flow through the heart. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the atrioventricular and semilunar valves throughout the cardiac cycle?
options: At no point in the cardiac cycle are all four cardiac valves simultaneously open — when the AV valves are open, the semilunar valves are closed, and vice versa
All four valves are briefly open during isovolumetric contraction to equalize pressure across all four chambers
All four valves are briefly open at the systole-to-diastole transition to prevent pressure spikes in the pulmonary circulation
The semilunar valves open first, briefly overlapping with the AV valves before the AV valves finish closing
questions.explanation:
At no point in the cardiac cycle are all four valves simultaneously open (A) — the AV valves and semilunar valves operate in strict reciprocal fashion: when one set is open, the other set is closed.

During systole, ventricular contraction closes the AV valves (mitral and tricuspid, held shut by papillary muscle tension) while opening the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) to eject blood into the great vessels. During diastole, ventricular relaxation allows blood to fill the semilunar cusps and close those valves passively, while the AV valves open to permit ventricular filling from the atria. This strict reciprocity ensures unidirectional, non-turbulent blood flow and prevents direct communication between the ventricular inlet and outlet.

Isovolumetric contraction is precisely the phase when both AV and semilunar valves are transiently closed (volume remains constant because no valve is open, allowing pressure to build). At the systole-to-diastole transition the semilunar valves close before the AV valves open — there is no simultaneous opening. The semilunar and AV valve events are sequential, never overlapping.

Slide 44 · Transcript 38:17

questions.text: A cardiology fellow teaching aortic valve anatomy explains that two of the three aortic valve cusps each harbor a coronary artery ostium, while the third does not. Which cusp of the aortic valve lacks a coronary ostium and takes its name from this absence?
options: Right cusp
Posterior cusp
Left cusp
Anterior cusp
questions.explanation:
The posterior (non-coronary) cusp (B) of the aortic valve has no coronary ostium — only the right cusp (right coronary ostium) and left cusp (left coronary ostium) give rise to coronary arteries.

The aortic valve has three semilunar cusps named for their orientation: right, left, and posterior. During diastole, blood flows back from the aorta and fills the cup-shaped sinuses above each cusp. Above the right cusp sits the right coronary ostium; above the left cusp sits the left coronary ostium. Blood filling these sinuses is automatically directed into the coronary arteries, explaining why coronary blood flow occurs during diastole. The posterior cusp has no coronary ostium — hence “non-coronary cusp” — and the aortic sinus above it simply fills and empties passively with each cycle.

The right cusp is named because it does contain the right coronary ostium, eliminating it as the non-coronary option. The left cusp contains the left coronary ostium and is similarly named for its coronary association. An “anterior cusp” is not one of the three aortic valve cusps (right, left, posterior); it is the name of one cusp of the pulmonary valve.

Slide 38 · Transcript 34:09

questions.text: A student tracing the aorta from its origin at the aortic valve notes that the ascending aorta gives rise to only two named vessels before becoming the aortic arch. Which vessels are these?
options: The pulmonary trunk and the superior vena cava
The brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid artery
The left subclavian artery and the left common carotid artery
The right and left coronary arteries
questions.explanation:
The right and left coronary arteries (D) are the only branches of the ascending aorta — they arise from the aortic sinuses (spaces immediately above the aortic valve cusps) before the aorta curves into the aortic arch.

The aortic sinuses of Valsalva are three dilations in the aortic root, one above each cusp of the aortic valve. The right coronary artery exits the sinus above the right cusp, and the left coronary artery exits the sinus above the left cusp. These are the only branches the ascending aorta gives off before it transitions into the aortic arch. The arch then gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery — none of these originate from the ascending aorta.

The pulmonary trunk arises from the right ventricle, not the aorta; the superior vena cava is a systemic vein returning blood to the right atrium — neither is an aortic branch. The brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid are branches of the aortic arch, not the ascending aorta. The left subclavian and left common carotid are also arch branches; the ascending aorta gives rise to neither.

Slide 39 · Transcript 42:57

questions.text: A student identifying cardiac veins on a heart specimen recalls that each major cardiac vein travels alongside a specific coronary artery. Which of the following correctly pairs each major cardiac vein with its companion artery?
options: Great cardiac vein with the right coronary artery; small cardiac vein with the LAD; middle cardiac vein with the right marginal artery
Great cardiac vein with the circumflex artery; middle cardiac vein with the right marginal artery; small cardiac vein with the PDA
Great cardiac vein with the LAD; middle cardiac vein with the PDA; small cardiac vein with the right marginal artery
Great cardiac vein with the PDA; middle cardiac vein with the LAD; small cardiac vein with the circumflex artery
questions.explanation:
The correct pairings (C) are: great cardiac vein with the LAD in the anterior interventricular sulcus; middle cardiac vein with the PDA in the posterior interventricular sulcus; and small cardiac vein with the right marginal artery along the right cardiac border.

Each cardiac vein travels in the same sulcus as its companion artery. The great cardiac vein is the largest and most prominent; it ascends alongside the LAD in the anterior interventricular groove and is the main tributary of the coronary sinus. The middle cardiac vein descends in the posterior interventricular sulcus next to the PDA. The small cardiac vein accompanies the right marginal artery along the acute margin of the right ventricle. All three ultimately drain into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium next to the IVC.

Option A reverses the great and small cardiac veins: the great cardiac vein travels with the LAD, not the RCA, and the small cardiac vein travels with the right marginal, not the LAD. Option B incorrectly pairs the great cardiac vein with the circumflex and swaps the middle and small vein-artery relationships. Option D inverts the great and middle cardiac vein assignments, placing the great with the PDA and the middle with the LAD.

Slide 49 · Transcript 47:00

questions.text: A student dissecting the anterior surface of the heart is trying to locate the left anterior descending artery. Her lab partner reminds her that the accompanying cardiac vein maintains a consistent positional relationship to the artery throughout its course. In which position will the cardiac vein be found relative to its companion coronary artery?
options: Superficial (on top of) the artery
Deep (beneath) the artery, between the artery and the myocardium
Medial to the artery, within the same fibrous sheath
Lateral to the artery, separated by a layer of adipose tissue
questions.explanation:
Cardiac veins lie superficially (on top of) their companion coronary arteries (A) — when dissecting from the epicardial surface, the vein will always be encountered first, with the artery lying underneath it in the coronary fat.

This consistent spatial relationship holds for all the major vein-artery pairs: the great cardiac vein lies superficial to the LAD, the middle cardiac vein lies superficial to the PDA, and the small cardiac vein lies superficial to the right marginal artery. In the dissection setting, this means you peel away the epicardial fat, encounter the vein first, and then find the artery beneath it. Recognizing this rule prevents inadvertently tearing the artery while trying to clear the vein.

The cardiac veins do not lie deep to the arteries — that arrangement would mean you must first identify and move the artery to find the vein, which is the opposite of what occurs during dissection. A shared medial fibrous sheath and a lateral adipose separation are not anatomically accurate descriptions of the cardiac vein-artery spatial relationship in this lecture.

Slide 49 · Transcript 46:29

questions.text: A 62-year-old man with known coronary artery disease develops crushing chest pain and discomfort radiating to his left arm and shoulder while shoveling snow. An ECG shows ST-segment depression in the lateral leads. Which pathway best explains why ischemic myocardium produces pain perceived as coming from the left arm?
options: Parasympathetic vagal afferents carry pain from the ischemic myocardium to the brainstem, which misreferrals it to the left arm
Sympathetic afferents from the ischemic heart travel along sympathetic cardiac nerves to T1–T5 spinal segments, which also receive input from the left arm and shoulder — producing referred pain
Phrenic nerve afferents from the myocardium refer pain to the T1–T5 dermatomes, producing the left arm radiation pattern
Intercostal nerve branches carry cardiac pain directly into the left brachial plexus, producing arm radiation
questions.explanation:
Pain from ischemic myocardium travels with the sympathetic cardiac nerves back to spinal cord segments T1–T5 (B); these same segments receive cutaneous input from the left arm and shoulder, so the brain misidentifies the pain as arising from those peripheral structures — the classic mechanism of referred pain in angina.

The cardiac sympathetic nerves originate from the sympathetic trunk at thoracic levels T1–T5 and carry efferent signals (increasing heart rate, increasing contractility, dilating coronary arteries) to the heart. They also carry visceral pain afferents back from the myocardium. When myocardial ischemia generates nociceptive signals, these travel along the sympathetic cardiac nerves to T1–T5 spinal cord segments. Because these same segments receive sensory input from the skin of the left arm, medial forearm, and shoulder, the brain cannot distinguish the source and attributes the pain to those peripheral areas — classic referred pain.

Parasympathetic vagal afferents carry reflex signals (baroreceptor, chemoreceptor) from the heart, not pain from ischemic myocardium — the vagus is not a pain pathway for cardiac ischemia. The phrenic nerve innervates the fibrous and parietal serous pericardium and refers pain to C3–C5 dermatomes (shoulder and lateral neck); this is the pathway for pericardial pain, not myocardial ischemia. Intercostal nerves carry sensory input from the chest wall and do not connect directly to cardiac pain pathways.

Slide 56 · Transcript 53:50

questions.text: A third-year student is asked to identify the most common valvular lesion responsible for a systolic ejection murmur — a harsh, crescendo-decrescendo sound loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space along the sternal border and radiating to the carotids. Which condition is the most frequent cause?
options: Mitral regurgitation
Tricuspid stenosis
Pulmonary stenosis
Aortic stenosis
questions.explanation:
Aortic stenosis (D) is the most common cause of a systolic ejection murmur — turbulent blood flow through the narrowed aortic valve during systole creates the crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space, the aortic auscultation point.

The aortic valve is auscultated at the right 2nd intercostal space along the sternal border. Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular outflow, forcing blood through a narrowed orifice during systole and generating turbulence that peaks in midsystole (crescendo-decrescendo). The murmur radiates to the carotids in the direction of blood flow. Over time, the left ventricle hypertrophies in response to the increased afterload. Aortic stenosis is the most frequent valvular abnormality and the most common cause of this murmur type.

Mitral regurgitation produces a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur best heard at the apex (left 5th ICS, midclavicular line) radiating to the axilla — not a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right 2nd ICS. Tricuspid stenosis produces a diastolic murmur, not a systolic one, auscultated at the left 4th ICS sternal border. Pulmonary stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur at the left 2nd ICS (the pulmonary auscultation point) — not the right 2nd ICS.
